paras: The burning of the Clarksville smallpox cabin took place on the night of April 17, 1882, when, by the account of Carter Russell, a Black smallpox patient, and his nurse, unknown parties ordered them out of his quarantine cabin outside Clarksville, Tennessee, on pain of death and burned it. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle reported that many residents believed the two had set the fire themselves, yet called the burning a "disgraceful act." Russell was later moved to tents under armed guard and died of smallpox there on April 26.

On Monday, April 17, health officer Dr. C. W. Beaumont confirmed a smallpox case in a cabin on Front Street in Clarksville. That day city officials sent Russell, with a Black woman to nurse him, to a pest-house about two miles out near the Paradise Hill road.

During the night, by the account Russell and the woman gave, unknown parties came to the cabin, ordered them to leave "under pain of death if they refused," and burned the building to the ground. The Chronicle added that "by many it is thought that they fired the house themselves," since Russell had been reluctant to leave town; he walked back to Clarksville that night.

On Tuesday no house could be had: residents refused to rent and threatened "all kinds of violence" to the patient and anyone moving him nearby. That night officials moved him to tents at an undisclosed isolated place under a guard "heavily armed with shot gun and pistols."
Russell died at the smallpox camp on Wednesday, April 26, and the Board of Health buried him nearby; no report of an arrest or investigation of the fire was found.

The episode survives in one local account, a Clarksville Weekly Chronicle article headed "The Small-Pox Case," much of which assured "our country friends" that no epidemic threatened. Though it repeated the rumor that the victims burned the cabin themselves, the paper condemned "such disgraceful act" and praised the authorities. Its brief notice of Russell's death, which did not mention the fire, was reprinted on May 2 by the South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville, Kentucky.

accounts.gist: Many thought the two set the fire themselves because Russell did not want to leave town.

framing.detail: The Clarksville Chronicle repeated doubt about who set the fire yet called it a 'disgraceful act' and praised the authorities' armed guard; most of the article reassured readers there was no epidemic.
The death notice, reprinted by the South Kentuckian, mentioned only the death, burial and absence of new cases.
